title: Has militancy in Jammu and Kashmir declined since 2019, and on which measure
summary: The government's central claim about Jammu and Kashmir after August 2019 is that militancy has collapsed. MHA's own table shows terrorist-initiated incidents falling from 228 (2018) to 28 (2024), security-force deaths from 91 to 31, militants killed from 257 to 67, and civilians killed from 55 to 14 in 2023 before rising to 26 in 2024. The counting instrument that produces those figures was rewritten twice by the ministry publishing them, in 2022 and 2023, with no methodology note in either report, and the two independent registers that could have produced a competing count - a legislature that could question police and public order, and a functioning local press - were removed over the same period. The record does not choose between the readings.
claimAtLaunch: MHA Annual Report 2024-25 para 15.9, verbatim: 'The security situation of UT of J&K has improved significantly. Organized stone pelting and protests have become things of the past.' The stated approach, from RS Unstarred Q.384 of 6 December 2023: 'The Government has a policy of zero tolerance against terrorism. The approach of the Government is to dismantle the terror eco-system.'
whatHappened: Totals computed from the AR 2024-25 rows for 2018-2024: 835 terrorist-initiated incidents, 731 encounters and counter-terror operations, 369 security-force personnel killed, 249 civilians killed, 1,142 militants killed. Infiltration attempts fell from 419 (2017) to 53 (2022), after which MHA stopped publishing the table. Tourist visits are offered as the normalcy proxy at 2.11 crore (2023) and 2.36 crore (2024), and President's Rule was revoked by S.O.4484(E) dated 13 October 2024. Against that: MHA has published 614, 417 and 228 as the number of incidents in calendar 2018, and 594, 255 and 153 for 2019, with no note accompanying either change; the trend is not monotonic on its own series (2021 at 129 above 2020 at 126); and the Pahalgam attack of 22 April 2025 killed 26 civilians in one incident, more than MHA's entire recorded civilian toll for 2023. MHA Annual Report 2025-26 was not located, so the whole of calendar 2025 - including the government's own classification of Pahalgam - sits outside the primary series here.
caseFor: Every measure the state publishes moves the same way and the largest falls are in the measures hardest to manufacture. Terrorist-initiated incidents fell 87.7 per cent between 2018 and 2024. Militants killed fell from 257 to 67, which is what a shrinking adversary looks like, and you cannot redefine your way to fewer bodies. Infiltration attempts fell from 419 to 53 and net estimated infiltration from 136 to 14. Above all, security-force deaths fell from 91 to 31 - and this is the government's strongest number precisely because it is the series the state has least incentive and least ability to understate: the dead are named, pensioned and publicly honoured, and no critic located in this phase offers a competing count. The independent press-derived register agrees with MHA on this measure year after year, within about ten per cent (91/95 in 2018, 80/78 in 2019, 63/56 in 2020, 42/45 in 2021). The restructuring objection also has a limit that fairness requires stating: the Annual Report table from 2022-23 onward does include civilians killed in counter-terrorism operations, per its own footnote, so the charge that the frame excludes one side's harm holds against the parliamentary series and against most political usage but not against the current table. And the corroboration extends beyond violence data: 2.36 crore tourist visits in 2024, an Amarnath Yatra completed by 5.12 lakh pilgrims, an assembly election held and President's Rule revoked.
caseAgainst: The instrument was rewritten mid-series by the party being measured, and rewritten for this theatre alone. MHA restated the incident series for 2017, 2018 and 2019 in the Annual Report 2021-22 with no note, then split it into two columns in the Annual Report 2022-23 with no note, then revised the civilian figures upward for 2018-2020 with no note - while the Left Wing Extremism table, in the same reports, kept an unchanged header throughout. The fall from 228 to 28 is read in public against a series that used to report 614 for the same year. Neither instrument has ever counted civilians killed by security forces outside counter-terrorism operations at all, and neither separates the two causes it now merges. The count itself is generated at the point of the killing by the force that did the killing, and the body is then removed to a distant graveyard: Amshipora put three civilian labourers into the 2020 militants-killed figure for eleven weeks. The verification machinery is inert - 506 magisterial inquiries since 1990, one completed and that report never submitted, no convictions - and both instruments that could have produced an independent count were removed over the same period: the J&K assembly did not sit from 2018 to 2024 and cannot legislate on police and public order now, the Kashmir Press Club closed in January 2022, and at least seven named journalists were held under anti-terror law between 2018 and 2023. And the trend is not the clean line it is quoted as: targeted killings of minorities and migrant workers rose in 2021-22, and one attack at Pahalgam in April 2025 killed more civilians than the government's own count records for the whole of 2023, in the district and the sector used as the normalcy proxy.
assessmentNote: Scored contested on the written definition - the evidence supports more than one defensible reading and the record does not choose. The split verdict below is deliberate and must not be collapsed: on the incident measures the two sides are working from different published numbers for the same object, while on tourism, turnout and Pahalgam they are weighting facts both accept.
differentFactsNote: The government's case is a set of quantities. The critics' case is a claim about the instrument that produced them: that it was restated twice without notice by the ministry publishing it, restructured for this theatre alone, and that the two registers capable of contradicting it - a legislature competent over police and public order, and a local press - ceased to operate over the same window. No single measure exists, or could be constructed from what is published, that places 'terrorist-initiated incidents fell from 228 to 28' and 'the counting instrument was rewritten by the party being measured and the independent checks were removed' on one ledger; the second is not a quantity. Granting the government its strongest fact in full - the fall in security-force deaths, which the independent register corroborates - leaves the critics' case untouched, and granting the critics their strongest fact does not make any published number wrong. This is the phase's structural finding rather than a feature of this record alone: for six of the nine quantities examined, a two-sided account of the conflict is an assembly the researcher makes and no source makes.

title: The J&K incident count: three published figures for 2018, and a composite named for one of its two parts
summary: MHA's headline count of terrorist incidents in Jammu and Kashmir was restated downward for 2017, 2018 and 2019 in the Annual Report 2021-22, then split into two columns in the Annual Report 2022-23. Neither report carried a note. The split revealed what the headline number had been: terrorist-initiated incidents plus encounters and counter-terror operations equals the old total exactly, for four years out of four - 228+189=417, 153+102=255, 126+118=244, 129+100=229. The figure used to demonstrate that militant violence declined was a composite in which roughly 45 per cent of the 2018 value was operations the state itself launched, published under a name that names only the other component.
whatHappened: Values as first published, from the reports themselves: 2014 = 222, 2015 = 208, 2016 = 322, 2017 = 342, 2018 = 614, 2019 = 594, 2020 = 244. The Annual Report 2021-22, posted 24 November 2022, gave 279, 417, 255 and 244 for 2017 to 2020 under the identical column heading and the identical introductory sentence, and did not restate 2014, 2015 or 2016 - it dropped them, so the old basis stands unrevised for those years and the new basis begins at 2017 with nothing on the page to mark the seam. The Annual Report 2022-23, posted 11 October 2023, replaced the single column with 'Terrorist Initiated Incidents' and 'Encounters/Counter Terror operations'. The mechanism behind the old wider basis is stated once in the entire corpus, in Rajya Sabha Unstarred Question No. 210 of 12 December 2018, verbatim: 'The number of incidents includes the violence committed by terrorists during anti militancy operations.' It never migrated into the series it describes. The restructuring was applied to Jammu and Kashmir alone: the Left Wing Extremism violence table keeps an unchanged header across the Annual Reports 2020-21, 2021-22 and 2022-23 and is never split by initiator, which removes the house-style explanation. For calendar 2018 five separately published and separately labelled incident counts exist - 614, 597, 417, 228 and 206 - of which the near-coincidence of MHA's 228 and SATP's 206 is arithmetic accident, one gating on who initiated and the other on whether anyone died.
caseFor: The composite is defensible on its own terms and MHA has said what it is. An encounter in which militants are present and firing is an incident of terrorist violence; the ministry told Parliament in December 2018 that the count includes violence committed by terrorists during anti-militancy operations, which is a statement of the rule, not a concealment of it. From the Annual Report 2022-23 the components are published separately, so the composite can be decomposed for every year from 2018 onward - a disclosure that went further than any predecessor and that is the reason the identity is now demonstrable at all. A ministry that narrowed its own headline figure by 197 for 2018 and 339 for 2019 moved the number in the direction that makes its own record look worse for those years, not better.
caseAgainst: An operation the state chooses to launch is not an event that happened to the state. Combining the two makes the series respond to the state's operational tempo as much as to the adversary's activity: an intensified year raises a number the government elsewhere wants low, and a quiet year lowers it for reasons that have nothing to do with threat. The reply of 20 July 2022 uses the composite to make exactly the claim the composite cannot support - 'There has been substantial decline in terrorist attacks from 417 in 2018 to 229 in 2021.' Two restatements of the same table in two consecutive report years, neither accompanied by a single explanatory sentence, and a restructuring applied to this theatre and no other, is not a disclosure practice a reader can audit. And the decomposition stops at 2018: nothing is published for any earlier year, so the years the series is most often quoted across cannot be decomposed at all. This case is available without disputing a single MHA number.
assessmentNote: The assessment vocabulary is built for measures with stated objectives and this record is a change to a reporting instrument. Scored no-objective on the written definition: nobody announced an objective for a reporting instrument, so no claim exists to test the restatement against, and the finding is firmly established either way. Explicitly not reversed - nothing that acts on the world was withdrawn, and a reporting practice altered by its own author is not a measure withdrawn by its enacting authority. title: MHA's 'Civilians killed' column changed meaning in 2023 and the footnote arrived fourteen months later
summary: The Annual Report 2022-23 raised MHA's published civilian death figures for Jammu and Kashmir - 2018 from 39 to 55, 2019 from 39 to 44, 2020 from 37 to 38 - under an unchanged column heading and with no footnote. The footnote explaining the change appeared one report later, in December 2024: 'Civilians killed includes civilians killed in terrorist-initiated incidents and civilians killed in encounter/counter Terrorism operations.' For roughly fourteen months a redefined series was published under its old name with no notice. MHA does not exclude civilians killed by security forces from this column; it absorbs them into a number that names no perpetrator, and it has never published a column for civilians killed by security forces under any heading in any year.
whatHappened: Three bounding formulas have been used for the same column name and none of them is in a table label. The Annual Reports to 2022-23 carried a bare heading with no bounding at all. Rajya Sabha Unstarred Question No. 371 of 20 July 2022 introduced its table as 'the number of security forces and civilians who died due to terrorist attacks since 2018' and gave 39 for 2018. Rajya Sabha Unstarred Question No. 2670 of 10 August 2016 used 'in these incidents'. The Annual Report 2023-24 footnote broadens rather than bounds. In every case the definition sits in surrounding prose rather than in the heading, which is the part of the document that does not survive transcription into any chart or aggregator. PIB's release of 7 February 2024 carried the definition inside the row label - 'Civilians killed in terrorist initiated incidents and in encounters' - ten months before the Annual Report footnote, while a PIB release of 7 December 2022 used the narrower 'in these terrorist incidents' for the same figure of 31 that MHA later footnoted as encounter-inclusive.
caseFor: A count that includes every civilian death connected to the conflict is more complete than one restricted to a single perpetrator, and the broadened basis is the one MHA now uses and has disclosed in writing on the face of the table. The revision moved the published civilian toll upward, which is the direction that makes the government's own record look worse, and a ministry concealing civilian harm does not revise its own figures up. The footnote, once it arrived, is unambiguous, and PIB carried the same definition inside a row label ten months earlier, so the disclosure was in the public record before the Annual Report caught up.
caseAgainst: A civilian-death count that names no perpetrator cannot answer the question a civilian-death count exists to answer. A reader of the current Annual Report sees one number and has no way to recover what share of it the state caused; a reader of the 2020-21 report saw a number that excluded those deaths entirely and equally could not tell. The change was made silently, in a table whose heading did not change, and the explanation followed fourteen months later. Nor does the broadened basis reach far: it covers deaths in encounters and counter-terrorism operations only, and not protest firing, crowd control, checkpoints or crowd-control munitions - deaths which MHA's own Annual Reports narrate in prose on the same pages as the tables that omit them, as the 2013-14 report does for four killed at Gool and a protester killed in CRPF firing at Gagran.
assessmentNote: Scored no-objective as a change to a reporting instrument rather than to a measure - no objective was stated at announcement for the column, so there is nothing to score it against. Not reversed: no intervention acting on the world was withdrawn, and a definitional change to a published column is not the enacting authority repealing its own measure. title: Six civilian deaths recorded to 31 July 2016: the boundary of MHA's civilian count, visible in one document
summary: Rajya Sabha Unstarred Question No. 2670, answered 10 August 2016, gave the number of civilians killed in Jammu and Kashmir to 31 July 2016 as six, and civilians injured as twelve. The answer was given five weeks into the unrest that followed the killing of Burhan Wani on 8 July 2016, during which large numbers of civilians were killed and thousands injured in security-force crowd control. The figures are not wrong: the annexure bounds itself, verbatim, to persons killed or injured 'in these incidents', the incidents being terrorist incidents. The Annual Report 2016-17 later put the full year at 15 civilians killed and wrote that there was an 11.76 per cent decrease in casualties of civilians compared with 2015.
whatHappened: The instrument's boundary is visible in this one document without any interpretation. The deadliest year for civilians in the period is recorded by the responsible ministry as an improvement for civilians, because the deaths it does not count are the ones the state caused. The same annexure carries a 'Civilians Injured' column - a quantity MHA has never published in an Annual Report in any year - and its value of 12 sits against the J&K government's own later count of thousands injured in the same unrest. The mechanism is general rather than particular to 2016: MHA's bounding formulas live in the sentence above the table and not in the column heading, so every automated extraction carries away an unbounded label and discards the bound.
caseFor: The answer is accurate to the question asked and states its own scope on its face. Parliament asked about terrorist incidents; the annexure introduces itself as counting persons killed or injured in those incidents; six is the correct figure on that basis. A ministry cannot be faulted for answering the question put to it, and the bounding sentence is printed immediately above the table for any reader to see. The Annual Report's 11.76 per cent comparison is a like-for-like comparison of the same bounded series year on year, which is the only comparison that series supports.
caseAgainst: The bound is stated in a place that does not survive use. Every chart, aggregator and press account built from these tables carries the column heading 'Civilians Killed' and discards the sentence, and MHA has never issued the figure with the bound attached to the label. The result is a published official count of civilian deaths in J&K that omits, by construction and without saying so on the face of the number, the entire class of deaths caused by the state - and the omission is invisible precisely in the year it matters most. The Annual Report then converts the bounded series into a claim about civilian safety in general: an 11.76 per cent decrease in civilian casualties, published for the year in which the state's crowd control produced the largest civilian toll of the period.
assessmentNote: Contested is used on its written definition: two defensible readings of one retrieved document, and the record does not choose between them. The finding here is the instrument's boundary, not a rival number - the civilian death toll of the 2016 unrest is not established in this phase from any primary document, and the finding survives intact without one.

title: Pellet-firing shotguns in Kashmir: the deaths counted, the injuries refused
summary: On 7 February 2018 MHA answered a Rajya Sabha question that asked for the number of protesters injured or killed by pellet guns in Jammu and Kashmir. It supplied a month-by-month table of deaths for calendar 2015 to 2017 - seventeen protesters killed, and two security-force personnel killed in law-and-order protests - and refused everything else in one sentence: 'Further details in the matter cannot be disclosed in the interest of the national security.' That single table is the only official Indian document located in this phase that puts harm to civilians and harm to the state's own personnel side by side on one page. It is the only pellet quantity located in this phase in a UNION government publication. It is not the only pellet quantity any government has published, and this record reports the counter-example itself: the Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister gave the Legislative Assembly bounded injury aggregates twenty-six days earlier, set out below. Those are a separate official publication on a different period and a different basis - not another reading of this series. The injuries, the munitions expended and the metallurgy of the pellets were all refused under the same exemption on the same afternoon.
whatHappened: The word 'pellet' occurs zero times in every MHA Annual Report from 2013-14 to 2024-25. Outside the flagship, figures exist and were produced under compulsion rather than published. The J&K Chief Minister told the Legislative Assembly, in a written reply reported on 12 January 2018 - twenty-six days before MHA's refusal - that between 8 July 2016 and 27 February 2017 in the Kashmir division 51 people were killed, 9,042 injured, 6,221 injured by pellets, 782 with eye injuries and 510 hospitalised. That route closed: the assembly was suspended in June 2018, dissolved in November 2018, and the assembly restored in October 2024 is barred by the Reorganisation Act from legislating on police and public order. In the High Court, on 11 May 2018, the Director of Health Services Kashmir filed a district-wise list of persons who had received pellet injuries, and the Medical Superintendents of SMHS and Bone & Joint Hospitals filed counts, natures of injury and procedures; the judgment of 11 March 2020 reproduces none of the numbers and dismissed the petition. Government Order No.61-Home of 2017 enumerated permanent and partial disablement over a 118-day window ending 2 November 2016 - a boundary the assembly's own figure crosses - and sanctioned Rs 0.75 lakh to 54 persons and Rs 0.50 lakh to 10. The CRPF told the same court it had fired 1.3 million pellets, 8,650 tear-smoke shells and 2,671 plastic pellets in the 32 days from 8 July 2016, so consumption returns demonstrably exist. The weapon was never withdrawn: MHA's own most recent authoritative statement describes an escalation sequence in which other munitions are used 'before the use of Pellet Guns', and on 30 July 2026 the Supreme Court declined a blanket ban on the ground that a Bureau of Police Research and Development advisory permits use in exceptional crowd-control circumstances.
caseFor: The choice was never between the pellet gun and nothing; it was between the pellet gun and a rifle, and the CRPF said so on affidavit to the High Court: 'In case this (pellet shotgun) is withdrawn, the CRPF would have no recourse in extreme situations but to open fire with rifles, which may cause more fatalities.' Before 2010 that was the recourse. The comparison is the state's own and it is stark: in roughly four months of unrest in 2010, policed largely without this weapon, around 112 civilians died; in the far larger and longer unrest of 2016-17, with 1.3 million pellets fired in the first 32 days alone, the Chief Minister told the Assembly that 51 were killed in the Kashmir division. More unrest, more force applied, fewer deaths - and the High Court found the same on the pleadings before it: 'because of use of Pellet Guns even though more protests become violent the loss of life is less'. The lethality figure is not an estimate but the government's own month-by-month series: seventeen deaths across three calendar years. Nor was the weapon adopted casually. It was ballistically tested at the Terminal Ballistics Research Laboratory on gelatin blocks selected to react as human tissue does; within eighteen days of the unrest beginning the Union government constituted a seven-member Expert Committee on alternatives, which reported within five weeks and whose recommendations MHA told Parliament had been taken into account; the result is a published escalation ladder placing PAVA, STUN-LAC and tear-smoke before the pellet gun. Two judicial forums have examined the demand for a ban on full argument and refused it, and the state paid ex-gratia for disablement without being ordered to.
caseAgainst: The weapon cannot be aimed. One cartridge releases between 360 and 600 metal pellets which scatter unpredictably, and the most a senior officer on the government's own Expert Committee would claim is that around 90 per cent strike below the waist - which concedes that roughly one in ten does not, at a rate of 1.3 million pellets in 32 days. The eyes are what is above the waist. The consequence has been measured, by government doctors, in peer-reviewed journals, using stated definitions, which is more than any government count offers: in one Srinagar hospital in four months of 2016, 777 patients were admitted with pellet-related ocular injuries, 76.3 per cent of eyes had open-globe injury, and final best-corrected visual acuity was counting fingers or worse in 82.4 per cent of eyes; in a prospective series at the same hospital 10.8 per cent of eyes had no perception of light at all; mean age in both is about 22. Amnesty International documented 88 people whose eyesight was damaged between 2014 and 2017, of whom 14 were women hit inside their own homes. And 'non-lethal' is the state's own word for a weapon that on the state's own count killed seventeen people. The trade-off argument requires knowing how many deaths were avoided, and no instrument located in this phase measures it. What has been measured is the harm - and the ministry that publishes the deaths refused to publish the harm on national-security grounds twenty-six days after its own state government had published the aggregate in a legislature, and four months before the same state's health department filed a district-wise injury list on affidavit. The two bodies that might have produced an independent count are gone: the State Human Rights Commission, which had produced the only severity taxonomy in existence, was extinguished on 31 October 2019, and the Assembly that extracted the only aggregate has been barred from the subject matter since. The one human-rights body that survives may not investigate the CRPF at all.
assessmentNote: Contested on the written definition, and the contest is not the one usually described. It is not mainly a values disagreement about proportionality: the state holds the measurements for both sides of its own trade-off, and the Union ministry publishes the term favourable to it while refusing the term unfavourable to it. title: Amshipora: a staged encounter, established by the Army itself, and its disposal
summary: On 18 July 2020 three men were shot dead at Amshipora, Shopian district, and presented as unidentified hardcore terrorists after a cordon and search operation. They were Imtiyaz Ahmad (20), Abrar Ahmed (16) and Mohammed Ibrar (25), seasonal labourers from Rajouri district who had gone to Shopian for orchard work. The bodies were taken 125 km to Baramulla and buried there, with no photographs released and no identification. Three families 160 km away filed missing-person complaints on 9 August; DNA matched in late September; the bodies were exhumed in October 2020. That the encounter was staged is common ground between the Army's own Court of Inquiry, the police chargesheet, the court-martial verdict and the Armed Forces Tribunal.
whatHappened: On 18 September 2020 the Army stated its inquiry had found prima facie evidence that powers vested under the AFSPA (J&K) Act 1990 were exceeded and that the Chief of Army Staff's Do's and Don'ts, as approved by the Supreme Court, had been contravened; the Court of Inquiry itself has never been published. The police chargesheet of 28 December 2020 named Capt Bhoopendra Singh and two civilians, alleged a Rs 20 lakh prize-money motive - which the Army contradicted on the record on 11 January 2021, stating it has no system of cash awards - and left documented gaps: no financial trail, no source established for the planted weapons, the statements of two majors never recorded 'in view of their transfer to the frontiers', the four soldiers who admitted firing listed as witnesses rather than accused. Court-martial proceedings concluded 16 January 2023; conviction on six charges including murder and a life sentence followed on 17 January. On 9 November 2023 the Armed Forces Tribunal suspended the custodial sentence and granted bail, holding that the confession was taken in close arrest contrary to the Evidence Act, that a conviction cannot rest on a co-accused's statement, that the Commanding Officer's claim of ignorance 'seems to be totally untrustworthy' given 391 rounds of AK-47 and 125 of LMG expended, and that there was evidence of deleted battalion WhatsApp chats - while expressly limiting its findings to the bail question. Two days later, on 11 November 2023, the Army's confirming authority confirmed the conviction and the cashiering. Whether a section 7 sanction request in respect of Capt Singh was ever forwarded to the Ministry of Defence, and its outcome, could not be established and must be treated as unknown rather than as refusal. The civil trial had not framed charges as at the last established position in July 2021.
caseFor: The institution investigated itself and did so seriously. Within a month of the families coming forward the Army convened a Court of Inquiry; within two months it publicly announced that its own personnel had exceeded AFSPA powers and contravened the COAS Do's and Don'ts - an admission no external body compelled. It then ran the matter to a court martial, convicted the officer on six charges including murder, awarded the maximum sentence available, cashiered him dishonourably, and confirmed both conviction and sentence. That is a functioning accountability chain, and it moved faster than the civil trial, which after several years had not framed charges. On the merits the prosecution's theory does not hold: the alleged motive was contradicted on the record by the Army, which has no cash-award system, and no money was traced. An independent judicial forum presided over by a former Chief Justice examined the record and found the conviction rested on a confession taken in close arrest contrary to the Evidence Act and on the statement of a co-accused, which cannot found a conviction - with nothing left if both are discarded. Suspending a custodial sentence pending appeal while leaving conviction and cashiering intact is ordinary criminal-justice practice, not impunity.
caseAgainst: Three labourers were taken, shot, dressed with planted weapons, stripped of their identities, labelled hardcore terrorists and buried 125 km away without photographs or names. Had three families 160 km away not filed missing-person reports, the record would have shown three dead militants for ever. That is not an aberration in the accounting; it is a demonstration that the accounting can be manufactured. Accountability then stopped exactly where it began to threaten anyone senior. The two majors most central to the case could not be interviewed because they had been transferred to the frontiers. The four soldiers who admitted firing were made witnesses, not accused. The soldiers who took the car were never identified. The source of the planted weapons was never traced. And when the Tribunal found the Commanding Officer's ignorance totally untrustworthy and found evidence of deleted battalion chats, the consequence was not that the inquiry widened upward - it was that the one convicted man walked out on bail. Meanwhile the civil prosecution, the only forum families can participate in, is immobilised by section 7. Whatever else this is, it is not a case that closed.
assessmentNote: Contested is used for the disposal and the scope of responsibility, not for whether the encounter was staged. That the three dead were civilian labourers and the encounter was staged is common ground between the Army's own inquiry, the police, the court martial and the Tribunal; treating that as contested would be behind the evidence.

title: Burial of encounter dead away from home districts, and who declares the identity of the killed
summary: Since April 2020 those killed in encounters in Jammu and Kashmir have been buried in remote graveyards rather than released to their families. No written order, circular or SOP establishing the practice has ever been published, and on the police's own account none exists: officials point to generic Disaster Management Act lockdown orders, a senior officer said in the same month that 'it's not a policy now but it should become a policy', and a lawyer acting for a family was told 'no written order has been given to us'. The stated reason moved from public health to prevention of glamorisation without the practice changing, and the practice was still operative in 2026 under an elected J&K government.
whatHappened: The practice first appears in the Keran sector operation in Kupwara, 1-6 April 2020, in which five militants were killed, neither police nor Army identified them, and all five were buried at an undisclosed location. The rationale predates COVID: a confidential J&K Crime Branch report of 2017 warned that funerals of local militants romanticise and glamorise them, and public funerals for foreign militants had been prohibited since October 2015. Three official counts of how many bodies have been buried under the practice circulate and do not reconcile - 158 for 2020 and about 180 for 2021 put before the Supreme Court in August 2022, about 140 for 2020 in one investigative account, and 'at least 580' since April 2020 as at February 2023 - and no published series exists. The bearing on counting is demonstrable rather than inferential. Amshipora put three civilians into the 2020 militants-killed figure for eleven weeks, and they were removed only because families 160 km away filed missing-person complaints. The Inspector General's own protocol makes identification conditional on a family learning of the death, obtaining a lockdown travel pass, reaching Srinagar in time and being believed by two District Commissioners, each of which is a filter that can fail without anyone recording that it failed. At Ganderbal in 2026 the police could identify the dead man only because identity papers happened to be on his body, and the family waited 75 days. The Supreme Court on 12 September 2022 set aside a High Court exhumation direction in the Aamir Magray matter while upholding compensation and grave access. The verification machinery behind contested killings is separately inert: the Hyderpora magisterial inquiry ordered on 18 November 2021 with a fifteen-day deadline has never been published, though the Lieutenant Governor sought two days to publish it on 7 December 2021, and a Ganderbal seven-day inquiry in 2026 had not appeared weeks later.
caseFor: Between 2018 and 2024 the security forces conducted 731 encounters and counter-terror operations and killed 1,142 militants while 369 personnel died in action. Against that volume the number of cases in which identity has been seriously contested and subsequently established as wrong is very small, and Amshipora is the case everyone names precisely because it is exceptional - exceptional in a second way too, because the state established it, the Army opened the inquiry itself and court-martialled the officer. Between 2016 and 2020 militant funerals were the single most effective recruiting instrument in the Valley, not private grief but staged public events with crowds mobilised across a wide radius; the Crime Branch said so in writing in 2017, and ending them is the most direct life-saving measure available. The safeguards are real and were stated with dated worked examples: religious washing and shrouding are performed, post-mortems and DNA are taken, families may identify and participate before a magistrate, and where identity is later established exhumation and handover follow, as at Amshipora in 2020 and Ganderbal in 2026. In Hyderpora the SIT reconstructed the sequence with physical evidence within six weeks and the two civilian bodies were exhumed and returned within three days without litigation.
caseAgainst: The base-rate argument assumes the denominator is knowable, and the state has arranged matters so that it is not. The dead are declared militants by the force that killed them, buried in a distant graveyard, unnamed and unphotographed; the check on that declaration is a family that hears in time, travels, is believed and gets DNA run. Amshipora is not a demonstration that the system self-corrects but of what correcting it takes - three simultaneous missing-person complaints, sustained press attention and eleven weeks. Ganderbal in 2026 shows the alternative: identification happened only because papers were in a pocket, and even then the family waited 75 days. Nor does the machinery for testing disputes function: 506 inquiries since 1990, one completed, that report never submitted, no convictions. Hyderpora is the model - an inquiry ordered within three days under public pressure, a fifteen-day deadline, a Lieutenant Governor who promised publication within two days, and no report ever; what was published instead was the police's own account of a police operation, clearing the forces. And a body is not a public-order problem: denying a family the right to bury its dead is a penalty imposed without charge, trial or finding, on people who have done nothing, by no published order that anyone can produce six years on. The COVID justification has outlived COVID by four years, and the police chief said so himself when he listed stopping glamorisation alongside stopping infection.
assessmentNote: Contested on the written definition, and the mixture inside it must be preserved rather than averaged. On the burial practice the disagreement is a weighting of one agreed fact; on the safeguards and on Hyderpora the two sides assert incompatible facts that no forum has resolved; and on the general question of identity one side asserts that the other's key quantity cannot be measured at all.
differentFactsNote: The state's case rests on a base rate - a very small number of established misidentifications against 731 operations. The critics' case is that the base rate is unmeasurable because of the burial and identification practice itself, and that claim is supported by a retrieved mechanism rather than asserted: identity is declared at the encounter site by the force that conducted it, before independent identification, and the body is then removed to a location that makes contestation costly. So the error in the series is structurally one-directional - mistakes flow from civilian into terrorist and not the reverse, because a body wrongly recorded as a militant is buried far away and unphotographed while a body wrongly recorded as a civilian would be claimed immediately. No measure exists, or could be constructed from what is published, that places the operations count and a declared-unmeasurable misidentification rate on one ledger; the counterpart is not unbuilt but unbuildable while the practice stands. What both sides do agree on is the strongest single fact here: in the one case where identity was conclusively tested, the official record had been wrong, and wrong in the direction of classifying civilians as terrorists.

title: Local recruitment into militancy: the quantity that is constantly quoted and has no instrument
summary: No MHA Annual Report has ever published a local-recruitment figure for Jammu and Kashmir. Established by exhaustive search across seventeen retrieved reports, 2008-09 to 2024-25: zero occurrences as a counted quantity, and none in any parliamentary reply retrieved. The subject appears only as a policy aspiration in near-identical prose for over a decade. What circulates instead are press-conference claims, principally by the Director General of Police, which conflict with each other: 2018 given as 187, as 218 and as over 200; 2022 as 100, 110 and 130; 2023 as 10 and 22. A quantity the Ministry describes itself as managing for fifteen consecutive years is not measured in the Ministry's own annual report.
whatHappened: The pre-2018 figures - 66 for 2015, 88 for 2016, 126 for 2017 - exist because an MLA asked and a Chief Minister answered in writing in the J&K Legislative Assembly on 6 February 2018. That route closed when the assembly was suspended in June 2018 and dissolved in November 2018, and the assembly restored in October 2024 is barred from legislating on police and public order. The post-2019 figures exist because the executive chose to announce them: the instrument changed from an answer to a claim. In October-November 2021, following the killing of two non-Muslim teachers in a Srinagar school, the J&K Police introduced the category 'hybrid militant', defined in their own words as part-time terrorists 'who were not on the official list of militants', with no previous record of involvement, identified as terrorists only after their first attack. MHA's Annual Reports never use the term - every occurrence of 'hybrid' in the seventeen reports is a hybrid meeting, a hybrid surveillance system or a hybrid street light. Whether persons so classified enter the recruitment count could not be established: no official statement either way was found and no journalist appears to have put the question. The recruitment figures fall from about 125 in 2021 to 100-130 in 2022 to 10-22 in 2023 to about 7 in 2024, so the steep fall postdates the category's introduction by one to two years, which is equally consistent with a genuine collapse and with a redefinition absorbing part of the flow.
caseFor:
Local recruitment has collapsed and every corroborating indicator moves with it. Militants killed fell from 257 in 2018 to 67 in 2024. Infiltration attempts fell from 419 in 2017 to 53 in 2022, and net estimated infiltration from 136 to 14 across the same years, before both series were discontinued. Over 1,900 overground workers were detained between 2019 and 2023, dismantling the recruitment pipeline itself. And the hybrid-militant category was not invented to hide recruits: it was coined to describe a real and novel adversary tactic, adopted precisely because conventional recruitment had become suicidal, and the police announced it publicly and repeatedly as their single biggest challenge for 2022. That is not how an organisation behaves when it is concealing a category.

This case has one further limb available to it in principle and not in fact. If most of the 67 militants killed in 2024 were foreign nationals, the fall could not be a reclassification of locals, because no redefinition produces foreign dead. Officials are reported asserting that composition and it may well be true. But MHA has never disaggregated "Terrorists killed" into local and foreign in any of seventeen years, and no figure in circulation has a retrievable basis - see the absence recorded on this record. The measure that would settle this argument in this side's favour is one the state does not publish.
caseAgainst: The recruitment series is not a series. It is a set of numbers announced at press conferences by the officer whose performance they measure; unpublished in any statistical return; absent from seventeen consecutive MHA Annual Reports and from every parliamentary reply retrieved; and internally inconsistent - 100, 110 and 130 for one year, 10 and 22 for the next, 187, 218 and over 200 for a third. There is no document to audit. And in the middle of the fall, the same police force introduced a category whose defining property is not appearing on the militant list: the men in it are, by the police's own definition, people who joined militancy without being counted as having joined militancy. Whether they are added back is a question nobody has answered, and nobody has been in a position to compel an answer since the J&K Assembly stopped sitting - which is exactly where these numbers used to be tabled, by a Chief Minister, in writing, to a named MLA.
assessmentNote: Scored no-objective: no objective was ever stated for a quantity that has no instrument, so there is no claim against which the absence could be scored. Note what is not contested and must not be recorded as a dispute: whether hybrid militants enter the recruitment count is a factual question with a determinate answer that exists in someone's hands and could not be obtained. It is an absence with a route, not a disagreement. title: Organised stone-pelting to zero: consent or suppression
summary: MHA told the Rajya Sabha on 24 July 2024 that organised stone-pelting incidents in Jammu and Kashmir ran 1,328 in 2018, 00 in 2023 and 00 in 2024 to 15 July, and organised hartals 52, 00 and 00, sourced to the UT of J&K. The series has never appeared in any MHA Annual Report in seventeen years, though the Annual Report 2024-25 asserts the conclusion in prose. Both sides accept the fall. They disagree about what the absence of protest is evidence of, and no additional fact decides it, because both accounts predict the identical observation.
whatHappened: The counted category is 'Organized' stone-pelting and 'organized' is nowhere defined, so unorganised stone-pelting is outside the count by construction and both 2023 and 2024 are reported as exactly 00 - a whole-year zero in a category whose boundary is undefined. The government's wider series, relayed and internally inconsistent, runs from 2,654 incidents, 112 civilian deaths and 6,235 civilian injuries in 2010 to zero on all three in 2024, with 302 hartal calls before abrogation falling to none; MHA is separately reported as giving both 759 and 1,458 for 2018 against the 1,328 of the primary reply, which is three official figures for one year and none may be picked. On the other side, MHA's own answer to Parliament records 765 people arrested in 190 cases for stone-pelting and law-and-order offences between 5 August and 15 November 2019 alone. Stone-pelting was never inside the 'Incidents' count at any vintage: 1,328 organised incidents in 2018 against a widest-basis incident total of 614 for the same year.
caseFor: Nothing prevents a Kashmiri from throwing a stone in 2024 that did not equally prevent it in 2016, when roughly 2,653 incidents occurred under a considerably larger and more aggressive security deployment. Repression does not explain the pattern: the periods of heaviest coercion produced the most stone-pelting, not the least. What changed is that the political economy of the street collapsed - the hartal calendars, the overground-worker networks that mobilised crowds, and the funerals that supplied the occasions. The consequences of that collapse fall on ordinary people and are measurable: zero civilian deaths and zero civilian injuries in stone-pelting incidents in 2024 against 112 dead and 6,235 injured in 2010. Those are Kashmiri lives and Kashmiri eyes. Schools and businesses that shut on 302 hartal calls a year now stay open. 2.36 crore visitors came in 2024, the Amarnath Yatra ran with 5.12 lakh pilgrims, an assembly election was held and President's Rule was revoked in October 2024. People who are being suppressed do not turn out to vote and do not host three crore visitors. Absence of stone-pelting plus presence of participation is consent.
caseAgainst: The fall did not follow a political settlement. It followed a communications blackout, a mass detention drive and the removal of the region's statehood: 765 people were arrested in 190 cases in the fourteen weeks after 5 August 2019. A fall in an activity for which the immediate penalty became preventive detention, passport and government-job denial, and FIRs against whole crowds, tells you about the penalty and not about the sentiment. More importantly, the instrument that would have registered continuing dissent was itself removed. From 2018 to October 2024 J&K had no Legislative Assembly; it now has one that cannot legislate on Police or Public Order and whose questioning of the Lieutenant Governor's discretionary functions can be restricted by rules the Lieutenant Governor makes. The pre-2019 figures that critics rely on exist because MLAs asked and Chief Ministers answered in writing; the post-2019 figures exist because the executive chose to announce them. The Kashmir Press Club closed in January 2022 and at least seven named journalists were jailed under anti-terror law between 2018 and 2023, one of them for reporting a contested encounter. Nor is participation the same as consent: high turnout in 2024 was widely read within Kashmir as a demand for the restoration of statehood - that is, as a vote against the arrangement whose success it is now cited to prove.
assessmentNote: Contested and deliberately held open. 'Some of both' is not a finding and must not be authored as one: the two accounts make one divergent prediction and it is testable over time, which is why this record carries a revisit trigger rather than a verdict.
differentFactsNote: Recorded false explicitly, because this is the cleanest weighting case in the phase and the temptation is to mark it true. Both sides accept every underlying fact: organised stone-pelting and hartal calls have gone to approximately zero; 765 people were arrested in the first fourteen weeks after 5 August 2019; the Assembly did not sit for six years and cannot legislate on police and public order; journalists were jailed; turnout in 2024 was high. Neither disputes any of these. The disagreement is entirely about what the absence of protest is evidence of - revealed preference on one reading, revealed cost on the other - and there is no additional fact that decides it, because both accounts predict the identical observation.

title: Infiltration into J&K: three quantities under one word, then no table at all
summary: MHA published an infiltration table in every Annual Report from at least 2010-11 through 2022-23 and then stopped, with no announcement. The Annual Reports 2023-24 and 2024-25 contain no infiltration figures at all while retaining the policy paragraph describing the multi-pronged approach to containing cross-border infiltration - the sentence about managing infiltration outlived the measurement of it. Over the same period the row label changed four times: an unlabelled 'Total' to 2013-14, then 'Total Infiltration Attempts', then a 'Successful' row, then 'Net infiltration (Estimated)', then 'Net Estimated infiltration'. MHA has never stated whether these are the same quantity.
whatHappened: Three distinct quantities are in play across three bodies - attempts and net estimated infiltration from MHA, and 'Infiltration Bid Eliminated' from the Ministry of Defence, which is LoC-only and Army-only by construction. They move in opposite directions under one underlying reality: if interception improves, attempts may be unchanged, bids eliminated rise and net falls. A series built by taking whichever body published a figure in a given year will show a decline that is partly an artefact of switching between them. The only two years MHA attributed the series to anyone attributed it to the Multi Agency Centre, an Intelligence Bureau body; from 2016-17 the attribution was dropped and the series continued. Net estimated infiltration for 2019 was published as 138 in three successive reports and as 141 in the Annual Report 2022-23, with no note, and net infiltration for 2021 is separately reported at both 34 and 24. The table's window also shortens: the Annual Reports 2018-19 to 2020-21 run the series from 2014, while 2021-22 and 2022-23 start it at 2017 and drop the earlier years from view rather than restating them. Into the measurement vacuum the Army speaks about a quantity it does not publish: the then GOC-in-C Northern Command declared 2023 the year of zero infiltration, which is an assertion about the net quantity made by a body that publishes only bids eliminated.
caseFor: The published rows are labelled and one of them is labelled an estimate on its face, so no reader is invited to treat 'Net Estimated infiltration' as a count. The apparatus that generates the figures is operational rather than statistical, and a border-management ministry is entitled to decide that publishing year-wise interception performance at the level of an annual report is not in the interest of border security - the policy description remains, in detail, and Parliament remains available to anyone who wants the numbers. The underlying claim the series supported is not in dispute on any published basis: attempts fell from 419 in 2017 to 53 in 2022 and net estimated infiltration from 136 to 14 on MHA's own figures, before any question of discontinuation arises.
caseAgainst: A series published for more than a decade was withdrawn with no announcement and no reason, in the two reports immediately after the last figure it carried was the lowest in the series. Nothing marks the discontinuation on the page; a reader of the current report cannot see infiltration at all, and a reader of the 2021-22 report cannot see 2014 to 2016. The labels changed four times without MHA ever stating whether 'Successful' and 'Net Estimated' are the same object, and MHA nowhere states how an attempt is detected or counted. The one year the series was restated - 138 to 141 for 2019 - carried no note, which is the same unannounced-restatement pattern the incident and civilian series show. And the policy paragraph survives while the measurement does not, so the ministry continues to assert that it is containing infiltration in a document that no longer says how much there is.
assessmentNote: Scored no-objective as a change to a reporting instrument - no objective was stated at announcement for the table, so nothing was claimed that its relabelling and withdrawal could be scored against. Explicitly not reversed: withdrawing a publication is not the enacting authority withdrawing a measure that acts on the world, and the border-management apparatus the table described continues to operate and is described at length in the same reports. title: The cumulative J&K conflict toll: thirty years, two populations, then discontinued
summary: Every MHA Annual Report from at least 2008-09 through 2020-21 opened its J&K security section with a cumulative sentence, ending at 14,091 civilians and 5,356 security-force personnel who had lost their lives since the advent of militancy, up to 2020. From the Annual Report 2021-22 the sentence is gone from all four subsequent reports, with no announcement. Two separate findings sit here: a stock series was discontinued with no successor, and in none of the thirty years it was published did it ever carry a militants-killed term.
whatHappened: Earlier values in the same sentence form run 13,880 civilians and 4,879 security-force personnel up to 31 March 2014, 14,024 and 5,273 up to 31 March 2019, and 14,054 and 5,294 up to December 2019, so the sentence changed its own period basis between fiscal and calendar closing dates without ever saying so. When MHA compressed the conflict into one sentence it ran two categories and omitted the third that its own annual table counted in the same section, every year. The components are still published annually; only the running total stopped. There has therefore never been an official cumulative total of conflict deaths in Jammu and Kashmir, only of two of the three populations, and since 2020 not even that.
caseFor: A running total since 1990 is a stock figure of limited analytical value and considerable capacity to mislead, resting on three decades of returns compiled under changing definitions and by changing agencies, and its closing dates drifted between fiscal and calendar years within the same sentence form. The annual components remain published, so nothing was concealed by dropping a summary that any reader can reconstruct from the tables. As for the missing militants term, the sentence was framed around lives lost to the conflict rather than around casualties inflicted in it, which is a defensible framing of an opening line and not an accounting claim.
caseAgainst: A ministry's own summary of a thirty-year conflict is the sentence most readers carry away, and for thirty years it was structurally one-sided in a direction opposite to everything else the ministry publishes: it counted harm suffered by civilians and by the state, and never once counted the population its own table on the next line reported killing. Nobody can reconstruct the running total from the published components either, because the annual series has been restated at least three times and the years before 2014 are on bases whose definitions are unestablished. And the sentence was not amended or corrected - it simply stopped appearing, in the same report year that restated the incident series, with no note in that report or any since.
assessmentNote: Scored no-objective as a change to a reporting practice - no objective was stated for the cumulative sentence, so its discontinuation has no claim to be measured against. Not reversed: what stopped is a disclosure, not an intervention acting on the world, and the definition of reversed excludes the withdrawal of a publication even by the authority that established it. title: Deaths in Army and central-force custody have no cell in any official instrument
summary: The national instrument for custodial deaths is Chapter 16A of NCRB's Crime in India, titled 'Custodial Crimes & Complaints Against Police Personnel'. Its unit of account is the State or UT police, and every row is a State or UT. There is no category, column, row or footnote anywhere in it for deaths in the custody of the Army, Rashtriya Rifles, CRPF, BSF or any other central armed police force. NCRB does not say it excludes them; it has no cell for them. In Jammu and Kashmir those are the forces most likely to be holding someone, so the quantity has no place to be recorded even in principle - and the J&K series in the same chapter breaks on 31 October 2019, when J&K appears as a State in the 2019 volume and as a UT thereafter with Ladakh split out.
whatHappened: The chapter's own bounding notes, identical across the 2019, 2020 and 2022 volumes, establish that the universe is police custody and lockup only and that the data are not NCRB's observations but 'As per data provided by States/UTs'. Table 16A.3 splits custodial deaths across seven causes, of which the single column corresponding to what most readers mean - 'Injuries sustained during the police custody due to physical assault by police' - registers one or two cases a year nationally: two of 85 in 2019, one of 75 in 2022, against suicide and illness which dominate. Any authored series must name which column it uses. The complementary instrument is statutorily capped: section 19 of the Protection of Human Rights Act 1993 confines the NHRC, for complaints against the armed forces, to seeking a report from the Central Government and then either dropping the matter or recommending, with the Act's investigative machinery disapplied by the opening words; and section 2(1)(a) defines armed forces to include 'any other armed forces of the Union', which pulls the CRPF and BSF inside that restriction. The 24-hour custodial-death intimation regime is addressed to District Magistrates and Superintendents of Police, so no Army formation or central-force sector command is an addressee. Before 31 October 2019 the position was worse: the Act applied to J&K only in respect of Union and Concurrent List matters, leaving ordinary policing to the State Commission, which on OHCHR's account had no jurisdiction over centrally controlled forces either.
caseFor: NCRB's architecture follows the constitutional allocation rather than a policy of omission. Police and public order are State subjects, Crime in India is compiled from State and UT returns, and every row is a State or UT because that is who reports to it; central armed police forces report through their own ministries and the Army through the Ministry of Defence, so a cell for them in a state-police compendium would have no reporting line to fill it. NCRB has never claimed the chapter is a complete national account of custodial death, and its own footnotes say the data are as provided by States and UTs and that States should not be compared purely on crime figures. The gap is a consequence of federal statistical design, and it is not evidence about how many such deaths occur.
caseAgainst: Whatever the reason, the effect is that in the one theatre where central forces do most of the holding, no instrument counts the resulting deaths and no instrument could. The absence is silent rather than declared - NCRB nowhere states that armed-forces custody is outside its frame, so a reader meeting a J&K custodial-death figure has no way to know what it omits. Nor is there anywhere else for the count to go: the NHRC may not investigate the forces concerned, its intimation regime does not reach them, and the one body that might have covered ordinary policing in J&K was extinguished on 31 October 2019 with roughly 630 pending complaints and a general transfer provision that cannot reach them - section 100 transfers proceedings pending before any tribunal, authority or officer to the CORRESPONDING body, and defines that as the body before whom the proceeding would have lain if instituted after the appointed day, which is empty by construction where the same Schedule repealed the enabling Act on that very day, leaving only a discretionary fallback no retrieved document shows was exercised. And within the frame that does exist, the category readers understand as a custodial death registers one or two cases a year for the whole country, which is a claim about the reporting rather than about the world.
assessmentNote: Scored no-objective on its written definition: the record finds something real - a structural absence established from the instrument's own architecture - and no objective was ever stated against which that absence could be scored. In particular no stated reason is attributed to NCRB, because NCRB has stated none - it simply has no category. title: AFSPA section 7: fifty sanction requests from J&K, none granted, and a decision rule nobody holds
summary: Section 7 of the Armed Forces (Jammu and Kashmir) Special Powers Act 1990 requires prior Central Government sanction before a member of the armed forces can be prosecuted for anything done in the exercise of the Act's powers. Since 1990 the J&K government has sought sanction in 50 cases. Sanction was refused in 47 and three remained pending as at April 2018. None was granted. When an applicant asked under the Right to Information Act not for the case files but for the procedure, norms, criteria and standards used to decide, both the Ministry of Defence and Army Headquarters answered that they do not hold the information; the Central Information Commission then sealed the case files under the national-security exemption in June 2020.
whatHappened: The figures come from a Ministry of Defence reply to Rajya Sabha Unstarred Question No. 1463 of 1 January 2018, corroborated by OHCHR's June 2018 report and by an RTI application reproduced verbatim in a CIC second appeal; the reply PDF itself could not be retrieved and the annexure listing the 47 individual cases has never been seen. On the decision rule the CPIO of the Ministry of Defence answered on 22 February 2018 that the information is not under his custody and should be treated as nil; the Under Secretary (AG-I) that it is not maintained or available in his section; and the CPIO for the Indian Army on 16 April 2018 that it is not available or held with the concerned agency of Headquarters. Both ministries denied custody of the same records. The CIC's final order of 5 June 2020 permitted access to the refusal orders in the 47 cases but refused the case files under section 8(1)(a), reasoning that the facts required a 'dynamic attribution to the meaning of larger public interest' by associating non-disclosure with it, and that 'indisputably, the larger public interest of the State (vis-a-vis its susceptibility to unrest) prevails over that of the alleged victims'. Separately, MHA told the Lok Sabha on 20 March 2018 that there is no proposal to amend or withdraw the 1990 Act. The Act itself is never named in any MHA Annual Report retrieved, and no disturbed-area statement for J&K appears in any of them, while AFSPA 1958 in the North East is reported every year at district granularity as a measurable achievement.
caseFor: Prior sanction is an ordinary protection for personnel operating under statutory powers in an armed conflict, and it exists so that criminal process cannot be used to paralyse operations or to litigate battlefield judgement in a magistrate's court. It is not immunity from accountability: the armed forces retain their own disciplinary jurisdiction, which in the one case where a staged encounter was established resulted in a Court of Inquiry, a court martial, a murder conviction and dishonourable cashiering - a faster and more complete disposal than the parallel civil prosecution achieved. The CIC did not seal everything: it directed disclosure of the refusal orders themselves, which is the reasoned part of each decision, while declining to open the underlying operational files. And a grant rate of zero over three decades is consistent with a screening mechanism working as intended if the cases put forward did not disclose an offence outside the exercise of the Act's powers.
caseAgainst: Fifty requests, forty-seven decided, none granted, over three decades, is not a screening mechanism producing a distribution - it is a determinate answer. And the decision rule that produced it is held by nobody: two arms of the same government each told the statutory information authority that the other holds it and that they do not, which means no written criteria for the exercise of the power exist or can be produced. The appellate body then declined to open the files on a reasoning that puts the State's susceptibility to unrest above the interest of the alleged victims - deciding, on the record, that the public interest lies in non-disclosure. In the one case where the state's own institution established that an encounter was staged, whether a section 7 request was even forwarded could not be established. The result is a provision whose operation cannot be examined, whose criteria do not exist in documentary form, and whose statute is never mentioned in the ministry's own annual account of the theatre where it applies - while the same ministry reports the retreat of the parallel Act in the North East district by district, every year.
assessmentNote: Scored no-objective as an institutional record rather than a measure - no objective was stated at announcement for the sanction regime, so the disposal record has no claim to be scored against. title: Two J&K security quantities lost their only legislative route in 2018, and it did not resume in 2024
summary: Two security quantities that MHA does not tabulate at all were on the public record only because a Member of the Legislative Assembly asked and a Chief Minister answered in writing: pellet injuries in the Kashmir division between July 2016 and February 2017, and year-wise local recruitment into militancy for 2015 to 2017. The J&K assembly was kept in suspended animation from 20 June 2018, dissolved on 21 November 2018, and did not sit again until October 2024. The assembly that returned is barred by section 32(1) of the Reorganisation Act from legislating on Police and Public Order, and the Lieutenant Governor may make rules prohibiting questions on matters affecting his own discretionary functions. This is not a gap in a series that resumes; it is the termination of an instrument, and it bit hardest on exactly the quantities the central instrument does not carry.
whatHappened: Three refusals in the restored assembly are documented, of unequal weight. In March 2025, at the first budget session in seven years, MLAs were barred from asking questions on terrorism, law and order, All India Services and related matters said to be in the domain of the Central Government, against roughly 1,300 questions submitted - how many were actually rejected, and on what individual grounds, is not established. In March 2025 the Speaker disallowed a discussion on the killing of three civilians at Billawar, Kathua, invoking section 32 and additionally a rule barring debate while a probe is pending. On 28-29 October 2025 the Speaker deleted a question asking the reasons for inordinate delay in ex-gratia and benefits under SRO-43 to the families of victims of violence, on the ground that the Home Department falls under the Lieutenant Governor's jurisdiction, and told legislators generally that they cannot ask questions pertaining to departments under the Lieutenant Governor's control. That third instance is a specifically requested figure, specifically refused, with an identifiable refuser, date, questioner and stated ground, on a question that sits squarely inside the security arc. Whether the Lieutenant Governor has in fact made rules under the proviso to section 46(1), or whether the Speaker's rulings rest on section 32 alone, could not be established, and the two are different things with different routes to challenge. A third quantity belongs with the two above and is better evidenced than either. PSA detention figures were answered on the floor of the same Assembly: in October 2010 the Chief Minister, who also held the Home portfolio, told the House that 724 people had been detained across 2009 and 2010, of which 322 between January and September 2010; and in March 2010 the Home Department, answering an opposition legislator, gave details of 334 persons booked under the PSA between 5 January and 14 February 2010 alone. Carry the contradiction with them - 334 in six weeks against 322 in nine months - because it is the state's own inconsistency showing in its own answers.
caseFor: The allocation is a straightforward consequence of the constitutional status of a Union Territory with a legislature, and it is the same allocation that applies elsewhere: where police and public order are Union subjects the legislature that does not hold them does not question about them, and the accountability route runs to Parliament, where the Ministry of Home Affairs answers and has in fact produced on request quantities that appear in no annual report - the organised stone-pelting series, the encounter counts, the injured columns. A Speaker's ruling that a department under the Lieutenant Governor is outside the House's questioning competence is an application of the statute, not a suppression of it, and one of the three instances was additionally justified on a pending-probe rule that would apply in any legislature. The Speaker himself has argued publicly for the narrower reading of the rule-making power, that it can only restrict matters requiring the Lieutenant Governor's discretionary action and only after consulting him.
caseAgainst: The two quantities that make this concrete are quantities the Union instrument does not carry. Pellet injuries and local recruitment into militancy appear nowhere in seventeen MHA Annual Reports; they entered the public record because an assembly could compel a written answer, and there is now no forum in J&K that can. Parliament is not an equivalent substitute, because MHA is simultaneously the answering ministry and the publisher of the figures - the producer and the consumer of the numbers became the same ministry on 31 October 2019 - and the one time MHA was asked directly for the pellet injury figure it refused on national-security grounds. The pattern of rulings since October 2024 runs toward the broad reading of the bar: three documented refusals in twelve months, one of them on compensation to families of victims of violence. And the underlying question of whether the bar arises from rules actually made or from the Speaker's own construction of competence has never been answered.
assessmentNote: Scored no-objective, and confined to answerability as it bears on whether security quantities can be counted - no objective was stated for the allocation of legislative competence, so there is nothing to score it against. The assembly, the elections and the restoration of statehood are outside this record's subject and are not scored here. SCOPE, made precise rather than weakened: the termination is SUBJECT-MATTER-SPECIFIC, not chamber-wide. It holds for security because s.32(1) removes Police and Public Order. It does not hold for revenue subjects: domicile and land sit within the UT legislature's competence - MHA told the Rajya Sabha on 11 December 2019 that the powers to make laws relating to land and property are vested with the Legislative Assembly of the Union Territory - and the restored Assembly demonstrably worked the route twice in 2025, extracting 83,742 domicile certificates granted to non-state subjects in April 2025 and 631 non-resident land buyers over 386 kanal in October 2025. That makes this a finding about s.32(1) rather than about the Assembly. title: The only instruments that ever named a perpetrator for civilian deaths in Kashmir, and their termination
summary: The Jammu Kashmir Coalition of Civil Society and the Association of Parents of Disappeared Persons published an Annual Human Rights Review which is the only instrument located in this phase that put both sides' harm on one page and named who caused it. Its 2019 edition records at least 80 civilians killed alongside 159 militants and 129 armed-forces personnel, and then splits the 80 by perpetrator - 19 killed by armed forces, 17 in cross-LoC shelling, 28 by unidentified gunmen, 6 by militants, 7 in explosions, one after being hit by a stone and one non-local in cross-firing. It leaves the largest bucket unattributed rather than forcing it. No edition after 2019 is retrievable, the coordinator has been in custody since November 2021, and the organisation's domain has been repurposed. After 2019 no instrument among those searched publishes the perpetrator split for civilian deaths in Jammu and Kashmir. (Bounded 2026-08-05, adversarial triage 2: this previously read 'no instrument of any provenance', which claimed the world while the search bounded a named few.) WITHDRAWN WORDING, recovered from the repository history in the backfill of 2026-08-06 and quoted so the correction can be checked rather than taken on trust: "The Jammu Kashmir Coalition of Civil Society and the Association of Parents of Disappeared Persons published an Annual Human Rights Review which is the only instrument located in this phase that put both sides' harm on one page and named who caused it."
whatHappened: The instrument declared its own measurement failure for the period it was last covering: since 5 August 2019 no proper research or documentation could be undertaken because of what it called a complete information collapse in Kashmir, so its final figures are a floor stated as such by the body that produced them. Its counted categories included cordon and search operations and raids - the quantity no official instrument counts at all. Its stated method was media monitoring, field verification, records obtained through the High Court registry and its own researchers' fact-finding. The termination is organisational rather than editorial: jkccs.net now redirects to an unrelated commercial page and every legacy deep path redirects with it, including the exact URL cited by OHCHR in its June 2018 report as the source for the Human Rights Review 2016 - a United Nations report's citation now resolves to a gambling site. Amnesty International India halted operations on 29 September 2020 with no in-country successor. On the official side there is no counterpart: MHA has never published a column for civilians killed by security forces; GTD covers non-state perpetrators only by definition; and UCDP has recorded Government-of-India one-sided violence in three country-years ever, none after 2002.
caseFor: A compilation with no formal methodology annex, resting on media monitoring and its own researchers' fact-finding, cannot carry the weight of an official series and should not be treated as one; its own provenance formula concedes it is based on media reports and independent verification, and it publishes no inclusion criteria and no counting unit. The organisation is not a neutral register but an advocacy body with a position on the conflict, and its figures were used as such. On the substance, the state's position is that the enforcement actions taken against it concerned specific alleged offences rather than its documentation, and the official instrument's coverage of civilian deaths has in fact broadened since 2019 rather than narrowed - the Annual Report table now includes civilians killed in counter-terrorism operations, which the pre-2022 series excluded entirely.
caseAgainst: Whatever its limitations, it was the only instrument that answered the question. Its discipline was in some respects better than either official register's: it named the perpetrator where it could and declined to attribute the largest bucket where it could not, and it stated its own measurement failure in writing rather than publishing a number that looked complete. The official broadening does not replace it, because the broadened column merges the two causes and names neither, so the one thing the terminated instrument supplied is precisely the thing no successor supplies. And the termination was not a publishing decision: the domain is gone, the coordinator has been in custody since November 2021, a named researcher was arrested in March 2023, the parallel international organisation halted Indian operations in 2020, and the state human rights commission that had produced the only official severity taxonomy was extinguished in 2019. The instruments capable of contradicting the state's count ceased to exist within four years of each other.
assessmentNote: Scored no-objective as an institutional record - no objective was stated at announcement, and what ended was an independent instrument rather than a measure of the state's. Not reversed and not failed: no measure of the enacting authority's was withdrawn and no stated objective went unmet - what ended is an independent instrument, and the record scores the consequence for measurement rather than the enforcement actions themselves, which are outside this phase.
